{{Short description|Circle of immediate corresponding curvature of a curve at a point}}
{{redirect|Kissing circles|Descartes' theorem on mutually tangent (kissing) circles|Descartes' theorem}}
[[File:Osculating circle.svg|thumb|right|An osculating circle]]
[[File:Osculating circles of the Archimedean spiral.svg|thumb|right|Osculating circles of the [[Archimedean spiral]], nested by the [[Tait–Kneser theorem]]. "The spiral itself is not drawn: we see it as the locus of points where the circles are especially close to each other."<ref name=gtt/>]]

An '''osculating circle''' is a [[circle]] that best approximates the curvature of a [[curve]] at a specific point. It is [[tangent]] to the curve at that point and has the same curvature as the curve at that point.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://math.libretexts.org/Courses/Monroe_Community_College/MTH_212_Calculus_III/Chapter_12%3A_Vector-valued_Functions/12.4%3A_Arc_Length_and_Curvature|title=12.4 Arc Length and Curvature|access-date=2023-09-19}}</ref> The osculating circle provides a way to understand the local behavior of a curve and is commonly used in differential geometry and calculus.

More formally, in [[differential geometry of curves]], the osculating circle of a sufficiently smooth plane [[curve]] at a given point ''p'' on the curve has been traditionally defined as the circle passing through ''p'' and a pair of additional points on the curve [[infinitesimal]]ly close to ''p''.  Its center lies on the inner [[Normal (geometry)|normal line]], and its [[curvature]] defines the curvature of the given curve at that point. This circle, which is the one among all ''[[tangent circles]]'' at the given point that approaches the curve most tightly, was named ''circulus osculans'' (Latin for "kissing circle") by [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz]].

The center and radius of the osculating circle at a given point are called ''[[center of curvature]]'' and ''[[radius of curvature]]'' of the curve at that point. A geometric construction was described by [[Isaac Newton]] in his ''[[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica|Principia]]'':
{{Quotation|There being given, in any places, the velocity with which a body describes a given figure, by means of forces directed to some common centre: to find that centre.|Isaac Newton, ''Principia''; PROPOSITION V. PROBLEM I.}}

==Nontechnical description==
Imagine a car moving along a curved road on a vast flat plane.  Suddenly, at one point along the road, the steering wheel locks in its present position.  Thereafter, the car moves in a circle that "kisses" the road at the point of locking.  The [[curvature]] of the circle is equal to that of the road at that point.  That circle is the osculating circle of the road curve at that point.

==Mathematical description==
{{See also|Curvature}}
Let {{math|''γ''(''s'')}} be a [[regular parametric curve|regular parametric plane curve]], where {{mvar|s}} is the [[arc length]] (the [[Differentiable curve#Length and natural parametrization|natural parameter]]). This determines the ''unit tangent vector'' {{math|'''T'''(''s'')}}, the ''unit normal vector'' {{math|'''N'''(''s'')}}, the [[Curvature#Precise definition|signed curvature]] {{math|''k''(''s'')}} and the ''radius of curvature'' {{math|''R''(''s'')}} at each point for which {{mvar|s}} is composed:
<math display="block"> T(s)=\gamma'(s),\quad T'(s)=k(s)N(s),\quad R(s)=\frac{1}{\left|k(s)\right|}.</math>

Suppose that ''P'' is a point on ''γ'' where {{math|''k'' ≠ 0}}. The corresponding center of curvature is the point ''Q'' at distance ''R'' along ''N'', in the same direction if ''k'' is positive and in the opposite direction if ''k'' is negative. The circle with center at ''Q'' and with radius ''R'' is called the '''osculating circle''' to the curve ''γ'' at the point ''P''.

If ''C'' is a [[regular space]] curve then the osculating circle is defined in a similar way, using the [[principal normal vector]] ''N''. It lies in the ''[[osculating plane]]'', the plane spanned by the tangent and principal normal vectors ''T'' and ''N'' at the point ''P''.

The plane curve can also be given in a different regular parametrization
<math display="block"> \gamma(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x_1(t) \\ x_2(t) \end{bmatrix} </math>
where regular means that <math>\gamma'(t) \ne 0</math> for all <math>t</math>. Then the formulas for the signed curvature ''k''(''t''), the normal unit vector ''N''(''t''), the radius of curvature ''R''(''t''), and the center ''Q''(''t'') of the osculating circle are
<math display="block">k(t) = \frac{x_1'(t) \, x_2''(t) - x_1''(t) \, x_2'(t)}{\left( x_1'\left(t\right)^2+x_2'\left(t\right)^2 \right)^{{3}/{2}}},
\qquad
N(t) = \frac{1}{\|\gamma'(t)\|} \begin{bmatrix} -x_2'(t) \\ x_1'(t) \end{bmatrix}</math>
<math display="block">R(t) = \left| \frac{\left( x_1'\left(t\right)^2+x_2'\left(t\right)^2 \right)^{{3}/{2}}}{x_1'(t) \, x_2''(t) - x_1''(t) \, x_2'(t)} \right|
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
Q(t) = \gamma(t) + \frac{1}{k(t) \| \gamma'(t)\|} \begin{bmatrix} -x_2'(t)  \\ x_1'(t) \end{bmatrix}\,. </math>

=== Cartesian coordinates ===

We can obtain the center of the osculating circle in Cartesian coordinates if we substitute {{math|1=''t'' = ''x''}} and {{math|1=''y'' = ''f''(''x'')}} for some function ''f''. If we do the calculations the results for the X and Y coordinates of the center of the osculating circle are:
<math display="block">x_c = x - f'\frac{1 + f'^2}{f''} \quad\text{and}\quad y_c = f + \frac{1 + f'^2}{f''}</math>

== Direct geometrical derivation ==
Consider three points <math display="inline">P_{0}</math>,<math display="inline">P_{1}</math> and <math display="inline">P_{2}</math>, where <math display="inline">P_{i} = (x_{i},y_{i})</math>. To find the center of the circle that passes through these points, we have first to find the segment bisectors of <math display="inline">P_{0} P_{1}</math> and <math display="inline">P_{1} P_{2}</math> and then the point <math display="inline">C</math> where these lines cross. Therefore, the coordinates of <math display="inline">C</math> are obtained through solving a [[linear system]] of two equations:
<math display="block">\left(\delta x_i\right)x_c + \left(\delta y_i\right) y_c = \tfrac{1}{2} \left(\delta^2 x_i + \delta^2 y_i\right) \quad i=1,2</math>
where <math display="inline">\delta u_{i}=u_{i}-u_{i-1}</math>, <math display="inline">\delta^{2}u_{i}=u_{i}^{2}-u_{i-1}^{2}</math> for <math display="inline">u=x,y</math>.

Consider now the curve <math display="inline">P=P(\tau)</math> and set <math display="inline">P_{0}=P(\tau-d\tau)</math>, <math display="inline">P_{1}=P(\tau)</math> and <math display="inline">P_{2}=P(\tau+d\tau)</math>. To the second order in <math display="inline">d\tau</math>, we have 
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\delta u_1 = & \dot{u}d\tau - \frac{1}{2}\ddot{u} \, d\tau^2\\
\delta^2 u_1 = & 2 u\dot{u} \, d\tau - d\tau^2 \left(\dot{u}^2 + u\ddot{u}\right)
\end{aligned}</math> 
and a similar expression for <math display="inline">\delta u_{2}</math> and <math display="inline">\delta^{2}u_{2}</math> where the sign of <math display="inline">d\tau^{2}</math> is reversed. Developing the equation for <math display="inline">x_{c},y_{c}</math> and grouping the terms in <math display="inline">d\tau</math> and <math display="inline">d\tau^{2}</math>, we obtain 
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\dot{x}(x_{c}-x)+\dot{y}(y_{c}-y)  &= 0 \\
\ddot{x}(x_{c}-x)+\ddot{y}(y_{c}-y) &= \dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2}
\end{align}</math> 
Denoting <math display="inline">\mathbf{r}=\overrightarrow{P_{1}C}</math>, the first equation means that <math display="inline">\mathbf{r}</math> is orthogonal to the unit tangent vector at <math display="inline">P_{1}</math>: 
<math display="block">\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{t}=0</math> 
The second relation means that 
<math display="block">\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}=1</math> 
where 
<math display="block">\mathbf{k} = \frac{d\mathbf{t}}{ds} = \frac{1}{\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2}} \begin{bmatrix} \ddot x \\ \ddot y \end{bmatrix}</math> 
is the curvature vector. In plane geometry, <math display="inline">\mathbf{k}</math> is orthogonal to <math display="inline">\mathbf{t}</math> because
<math display="block">\mathbf{t} \cdot \mathbf{k} = \mathbf{t}\frac{d\mathbf{t}}{ds} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{ds}(\mathbf{t} \cdot \mathbf{t}) = \frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{ds}(1) = 0</math> Therefore <math display="inline">\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} = kr</math> and the radius of the osculating circle is precisely the inverse of the curvature.

Solving the equation for the coordinates of <math display="inline">C</math>, we find 
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
x_{c} - x  = & \frac{\dot{y}\left(\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2}\right)}{\dot{y}\ddot{x}-\dot{x}\ddot{y}}\\
y_{c} - y  = & \frac{-\dot{x}\left(\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2}\right)}{\dot{y}\ddot{x}-\dot{x}\ddot{y}}
\end{aligned}</math>

== Osculating circle as a  minimization problem ==
Consider a curve <math display="inline">C</math> defined intrinsically by the equation
<math display="block">f(x,y) = 0</math> 
which we can envision as the section of the surface <math display="inline">z = f(x,y)</math> by the plane <math display="inline">z = 0</math>. 
The normal <math display="inline">\mathbf{n}</math> to the curve at a point <math display="inline">P_{0}=(x_{0},y_{0})</math> is the gradient at this point <math display="block">\mathbf{n}=(f_{x},f_{y})</math> 
Therefore, the centers of the tangent circles <math display="inline"> B_{\alpha}</math> are given by 
<math display="block">X_c = x_0 - \alpha f_x \,\, ;\,\, Y_c = y_0 - \alpha f_y </math>
where <math display="inline">\alpha</math> is parameter. For a given <math display="inline">\alpha,</math>the radius <math display="inline">R</math> of <math display="inline">B_{\alpha}</math> is <math display="block">R^2 = \alpha^2 (f_x^2 + f_y^2)</math> We wish to find, among all possible circles <math display="inline">B_{\alpha}</math>, the one that ''matches'' best the curve.

The coordinates of a point <math display="inline">P_{1} \in B_{\alpha}</math> can be written as 
<math display="block">x_1 = X_c +R\cos\theta\,\,;\,\, y_1 = Y_c + R\sin\theta</math> 
where for <math display="inline">\theta=\theta_{0}</math>, <math display="inline">P_1 = P_0</math>, i.e. 
<math display="block">R\cos\theta_{0}=\alpha f_{x}\,\,;\,\,R\sin\theta_{0}=\alpha f_y</math> 
Consider now a point <math display="inline">P_{1}\in B_{\alpha}</math> close to <math display="inline">P_0</math>, where its "angle" is <math display="inline">\theta_{1} = \theta_{0} + d\theta</math>. Developing the [[trigonometric functions]] to the second order in <math display="inline">d\theta</math> and using the above relations, coordinates of <math>P_1</math> are 
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
x_1 = & x_0 - \alpha f_y d\theta - \tfrac{1}{2} \alpha f_x \left(d\theta\right)^2\\
y_1 = & y_0 + \alpha f_x d\theta - \tfrac{1}{2} \alpha f_y \left(d\theta\right)^2
\end{aligned}</math> 
We can now evaluate the function <math display="inline">f</math> at the point <math display="inline">P_{1}</math> and its variation  <math>f(x_1, y_1) - f(x_0, y_0)</math>. 
The variation is zero to the first order in <math display="inline">d\theta</math> by construction (to the first order in <math display="inline">\theta</math>, <math display="inline">P_{1}</math> is on the tangent line to the curve <math display="inline">C</math>). The variation proportional to <math> (d\theta)^2</math> is
<math display="block">df = -\frac{1}{2} \alpha \left(f_x^2 + f_y^2\right) + \frac{1}{2}\alpha^{2}\left(f_y^2 f_{xx} + f_x^2 f_{yy} - f_x f_y f_{xy}\right)</math> 
and this variation is zero if we choose 
<math display="block">\alpha = \frac{f_x^2 + f_y^2}{f_y^2 f_{xx} + f_x^2 f_{yy} - f_x f_y f_{xy}}</math> 
Therefore the radius of the osculating circle is 
<math display="block">R=\left| \frac{\left(f_x^2 + f_y^2\right)^{3/2}}{\left(f_y^2 f_{xx} + f_x^2 f_{yy} - f_x f_y f_{xy}\right)} \right|</math>

For an explicit function <math> f(x,y) = y - g(x) </math>, we find the results of the preceding section.

==Properties==

For a curve ''C'' given by a sufficiently smooth parametric equations (twice continuously differentiable), the osculating circle may be obtained by a limiting procedure: it is the limit of the circles passing through three distinct points on ''C'' as these points approach ''P''.<ref name=Lamb>Actually, point ''P'' plus two additional points, one on either side of ''P'' will do. See Lamb (on line): {{cite book |title=An Elementary Course of Infinitesimal Calculus |author=Horace Lamb |page=[https://archive.org/details/anelementarycou01lambgoog/page/n429 406] |url=https://archive.org/details/anelementarycou01lambgoog |quote=osculating circle. |publisher=University Press |year=1897}}</ref> This is entirely analogous to the construction of the [[tangent]] to a curve as a limit of the secant lines through pairs of distinct points on ''C'' approaching ''P''.

The osculating circle ''S'' to a plane curve ''C'' at a regular point ''P'' can be characterized by the following properties:
* The circle ''S'' passes through ''P''.
* The circle ''S'' and the curve ''C'' have the [[tangent lines to circles|common tangent]] line at ''P'', and therefore the common normal line.
* Close to ''P'', the distance between the points of the curve ''C'' and the circle ''S'' in the normal direction decays as the cube or a higher power of the distance to ''P'' in the tangential direction.
This is usually expressed as "the curve and its osculating circle have the second or higher order [[Contact (mathematics)|contact]]" at ''P''. Loosely speaking, the vector functions representing ''C'' and ''S'' agree together with their first and second derivatives at ''P''.

If the derivative of the curvature with respect to ''s'' is nonzero at ''P'' then the osculating circle crosses the curve ''C'' at ''P''. Points ''P'' at which the derivative of the curvature is zero are called [[vertex (curve)|vertices]]. If ''P'' is a vertex then ''C'' and its osculating circle have contact of order at least three. If, moreover, the curvature has a non-zero [[local maximum]] or minimum at ''P'' then the osculating circle touches the curve ''C'' at ''P'' but does not cross it.

The curve ''C'' may be obtained as the [[envelope (mathematics)|envelope]] of the one-parameter family of its osculating circles. Their centers, i.e. the centers of curvature,  form another curve, called the ''[[evolute]]'' of ''C''. Vertices of ''C'' correspond to singular points on its evolute.

Within any arc of a curve ''C'' within which the curvature is monotonic (that is, away from any [[vertex (curve)|vertex]] of the curve), the osculating circles are all disjoint and nested within each other. This result is known as the [[Tait-Kneser theorem]].<ref name=gtt>{{cite journal|last1=Ghys|first1=Étienne|author1-link=Étienne Ghys|last2=Tabachnikov|first2=Sergei| author2-link=Sergei Tabachnikov|last3=Timorin|first3=Vladlen|arxiv=1207.5662|doi=10.1007/s00283-012-9336-6|issue=1|journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer|mr=3041992|pages=61–66|title=Osculating curves: around the Tait-Kneser theorem|volume=35|year=2013 | s2cid=18183204}}</ref>

==Examples==

===Parabola===
[[File:Parabola circle.svg|thumb|250px|The osculating circle of the parabola at its vertex has radius 0.5 and fourth order contact.]]
For the parabola
<math display="block">\gamma(t) = \begin{bmatrix} t \\ t^2 \end{bmatrix}</math>
the radius of curvature is
<math display="block">R(t)= \left| \frac{ \left(1 + 4 t^2 \right)^{3/2}}{2} \right| </math>
At the vertex <math>\gamma(0) = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\0 \end{bmatrix}</math>  the radius of curvature equals {{math|1=''R''(0) = 0.5}} (see figure). The parabola has fourth order contact with its osculating circle there. For large {{mvar|t}} the radius of curvature increases ~ {{math|''t''{{i sup|3}}}}, that is, the curve straightens more and more.

===Lissajous curve===
[[File:Lissajous-Curve+OsculatingCircle+3vectors animated.gif|Animation of the osculating circle to a Lissajous curve|frame]]
A [[Lissajous curve]] with ratio of frequencies (3:2) can be parametrized as follows
:<math> \gamma(t) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(3t) \\ \sin(2t) \end{bmatrix}. </math>

It has signed curvature {{math|''k''(''t'')}}, normal unit vector {{math|''N''(''t'')}} and radius of curvature {{math|''R''(''t'')}} given by
<math display="block">k(t) = \frac{6\cos(t)(8(\cos t)^4-10(\cos t)^2+5)}{\left(232(\cos t)^4-97(\cos t)^2 + 13 - 144(\cos t)^6\right)^{3/2}} \,, </math>
<math display="block">N(t) = \frac{1}{\| \gamma'(t)\|} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -2\cos(2t) \\ -3\sin(3t) \end{bmatrix}</math>
and
<math display="block">R(t) = \left| \frac{\left(232\cos^4(t) -97 \cos^2(t) + 13 - 144 \cos^6(t)\right)^{3/2}}{6\cos(t)\left(8\cos^4(t) - 10\cos^2(t) +5\right)} \right|.</math>

See the figure for an animation. There the "acceleration vector" is the second derivative <math display="inline">\frac{d^2\gamma}{ds^2}</math> with respect to the [[arc length]] {{mvar|s}}.

===Cycloid===
[[File:Cycloid osculating circle evolute 2.gif|350px|thumb|Cycloid (blue), its osculating circle (red) and evolute (green).]]
A [[cycloid]] with radius {{mvar|r}} can be parametrized as follows:
<math display="block"> \gamma(t) = \begin{bmatrix} r\left(t - \sin t\right) \\ r\left(1 - \cos t\right) \end{bmatrix} </math>

Its curvature is given by the following formula:<ref>{{MathWorld |title=Cycloid |id=Cycloid}}</ref>
<math display="block">\kappa(t) = - \frac{\left| \csc \left( \frac{t}{2} \right) \right|}{4r}</math>
which gives:
<math display="block">R(t) = \frac{4r}{\left| \csc \left( \frac{t}{2} \right) \right|}</math>
